overview: This is the modern Irish state, not a Kingdom of Ireland. Its constitutional development began before the first 1938 map snapshot: the Irish Free State dates to 1922, followed by the 1937 Constitution. Electricity, schooling, water supplies and community sport show how public changes reached ordinary households.

periods.title: Before the first snapshot
periods.summary: The Free State constitution was adopted in 1922; a new constitution followed in 1937.

periods.title: State building and everyday change
periods.summary: The 1949 republic legislation, rural electrification and expanded educational provision changed institutions and opportunities.

periods.title: European membership and continuing society
periods.summary: Ireland entered the European Communities in 1973; its state and cultural life continue.

sections.title: A state, a name and public decisions

items.text: The 1922 Constitution Committee left records of its work on the Irish Free State's institutions. Constitutions are written through discussion and choices, not simply discovered ready-made. This founding phase predates the atlas's 1938 beginning.

The Republic of Ireland Act came into operation on 18 April 1949. The enactment and its commencement are different dates. This is a constitutional milestone in an already existing state, not the sudden appearance of Irish people or culture.

Éire is ainm don Stát means “The name of the State is Éire.” It comes from Article 4 of the Constitution in the official online Irish text, which uses modern standardized spelling. Irish language and Latin script should not be confused with each other.

sections.title: Electricity and the work of a home

items.text: The Rural Electrification Scheme began in 1946; its first pole was erected at Kilsallaghan, County Dublin, on 5 November. Bringing power to scattered homes required surveying, poles, wires and crews. A switch on the wall was the visible end of a much larger job.

The 1957 ESB film More Power to the Farmer shows hand washing, butter churning and carrying water in buckets. Its demonstrations promoted electrical alternatives. This was a persuasive company film, so its scenes are evidence of an argument for change, not a neutral picture of every farm.

The film also shows customers asking about charges and deciding whether to sign up. A new machine could promise less work while still raising questions about cost. Household modernization depended on decisions as well as technology.

The 1961 census counted 301,774 farm dwellings; 237,904 obtained water from a well, fountain, pump or other source rather than a piped supply. These figures concern farm dwellings specifically. They show why fetching water remained a major practical issue.

In that same farm-dwelling table, only 30,943 had use of a fixed bath and 31,500 a hot-water tap. A house with electrical light did not automatically have a modern bathroom. Different improvements reached families at different times.

sections.title: Getting to school and playing together

items.text: A 1967 Department of Education circular set out free post-primary education. Removing tuition costs changed the possibilities facing families, although educational access involves more than the price of lessons.

The 1967-68 public accounts record free school transport from 1 April 1967. For a pupil living far from school, a practical way to get there mattered alongside classroom policy. A bus route could be part of an educational achievement.

Hurling and camogie connect playing skills with clubs, families and local communities. UNESCO's 2018 description emphasizes learning through practice and coaching. It records a living tradition, not one frozen version played identically in every century.

The same tradition depends on volunteers who coach, organize teams and help clubs operate. Social life includes the work surrounding a match, as well as the players on the field. The final score is only part of what a community makes together.

ending.text: Ireland continues as a sovereign state. Constitutional milestones in 1922, 1937 and 1949 describe changes in its institutions, while membership of the European Communities began in 1973. Its people, languages, public institutions and everyday traditions continue to develop.
